{{Correlation and covariance}}
{{Confuse|Covariance matrix}}
{{short description|Type of matrix in probability theory and statistics}}
In [[probability theory]] and [[statistics]], a '''cross-covariance matrix''' is a [[Matrix (mathematics)|matrix]] whose element in the ''i'', ''j'' position is the [[covariance]] between the ''i''-th element of a [[random vector]] and ''j''-th element of another random vector.
When the two random vectors are the same, the cross-covariance matrix is referred to as [[covariance matrix]].
A random vector is a [[random variable]] with multiple dimensions. Each element of the vector is a [[Scalar (mathematics)|scalar]] random variable. Each element has either a finite number of ''observed'' empirical values or a finite or infinite number of ''potential'' values. The potential values are specified by a theoretical [[joint probability distribution]]. Intuitively, the cross-covariance matrix generalizes the notion of covariance to multiple dimensions.

The cross-covariance matrix of two random vectors <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> is typically denoted by <math>\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}}</math> or <math>\Sigma_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}}</math>.

==Definition==
For [[random vector]]s <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math>, each containing [[random element]]s whose [[expected value]] and [[variance]] exist, the '''cross-covariance matrix''' of <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> is defined by<ref name=Gubner>{{cite book |first=John A. |last=Gubner |year=2006 |title=Probability and Random Processes for Electrical and Computer Engineers |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-86470-1}}</ref>{{rp|p=336}}

{{Equation box 1
|indent =
|title=
|equation = {{NumBlk||<math>\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}} = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{\mu_X})(\mathbf{Y}-\mathbf{\mu_Y})^{\rm T}]</math>|{{EquationRef|Eq.1}}}}
|cellpadding= 6
|border
|border colour = #0073CF
|background colour=#F5FFFA}}

where <math>\mathbf{\mu_X} = \operatorname{E}[\mathbf{X}]</math> and <math>\mathbf{\mu_Y} = \operatorname{E}[\mathbf{Y}]</math> are vectors containing the expected values of <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math>. The vectors <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> need not have the same dimension, and either might be a scalar value.

The cross-covariance matrix is the matrix whose <math>(i,j)</math> entry is the [[covariance]]

:<math>\operatorname{K}_{X_i Y_j} = \operatorname{cov}[X_i, Y_j] = \operatorname{E}[(X_i - \operatorname{E}[X_i])(Y_j - \operatorname{E}[Y_j])]</math>

between the ''i''-th element of <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and the ''j''-th element of <math>\mathbf{Y}</math>. This gives the following component-wise definition of the cross-covariance matrix.

:<math>
\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}}=
\begin{bmatrix}
 \mathrm{E}[(X_1 - \operatorname{E}[X_1])(Y_1 - \operatorname{E}[Y_1])] & \mathrm{E}[(X_1 - \operatorname{E}[X_1])(Y_2 - \operatorname{E}[Y_2])] & \cdots & \mathrm{E}[(X_1 - \operatorname{E}[X_1])(Y_n - \operatorname{E}[Y_n])] \\ \\
 \mathrm{E}[(X_2 - \operatorname{E}[X_2])(Y_1 - \operatorname{E}[Y_1])] & \mathrm{E}[(X_2 - \operatorname{E}[X_2])(Y_2 - \operatorname{E}[Y_2])] & \cdots & \mathrm{E}[(X_2 - \operatorname{E}[X_2])(Y_n - \operatorname{E}[Y_n])] \\ \\
 \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \\
 \mathrm{E}[(X_m - \operatorname{E}[X_m])(Y_1 - \operatorname{E}[Y_1])] & \mathrm{E}[(X_m - \operatorname{E}[X_m])(Y_2 - \operatorname{E}[Y_2])] & \cdots & \mathrm{E}[(X_m - \operatorname{E}[X_m])(Y_n - \operatorname{E}[Y_n])]
\end{bmatrix}
</math>

==Example==
For example, if <math>\mathbf{X} = \left( X_1,X_2,X_3 \right)^{\rm T}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y} = \left( Y_1,Y_2 \right)^{\rm T}</math> are random vectors, then
<math> \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) </math> is a <math>3 \times 2</math> matrix whose <math>(i,j)</math>-th entry is <math>\operatorname{cov}(X_i,Y_j)</math>.

==Properties==
For the cross-covariance matrix, the following basic properties apply:<ref name=taboga>{{cite web |last1=Taboga |first1=Marco |url=http://www.statlect.com/varian2.htm |title=Lectures on probability theory and mathematical statistics |year=2010}}</ref>

# <math> \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) = \operatorname{E}[\mathbf{X} \mathbf{Y}^{\rm T}] - \mathbf{\mu_X} \mathbf{\mu_Y}^{\rm T} </math>
# <math> \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{Y},\mathbf{X})^{\rm T}</math>
# <math> \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X_1} + \mathbf{X_2},\mathbf{Y}) = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X_1},\mathbf{Y}) + \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X_2}, \mathbf{Y})</math>
# <math>\operatorname{cov}(A\mathbf{X}+ \mathbf{a}, B^{\rm T}\mathbf{Y} + \mathbf{b}) = A\, \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X}, \mathbf{Y}) \,B</math>
# If <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> are independent (or somewhat less restrictedly, if every random variable in <math>\mathbf{X}</math> is uncorrelated with every random variable in <math>\mathbf{Y}</math>), then <math>\operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{X},\mathbf{Y}) = 0_{p\times q}</math>

where <math>\mathbf{X}</math>, <math>\mathbf{X_1}</math> and <math>\mathbf{X_2}</math> are random <math>p \times 1</math> vectors, <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> is a random <math>q \times 1</math> vector, <math>\mathbf{a}</math> is a <math>q \times 1</math> vector, <math>\mathbf{b}</math> is a <math>p \times 1</math> vector, <math>A</math> and <math>B</math> are <math>q \times p</math> matrices of constants, and <math>0_{p\times q}</math> is a <math>p \times q</math> matrix of zeroes.

==Definition for complex random vectors==
{{Main|Complex random vector#Cross-covariance matrix and pseudo-cross-covariance matrix}}
If <math>\mathbf{Z}</math> and <math>\mathbf{W}</math> are complex random vectors, the definition of the cross-covariance matrix is slightly changed. Transposition is replaced by [[Conjugate transpose|Hermitian transposition]]:

:<math>\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{Z},\mathbf{W}) \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{\mu_Z})(\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{\mu_W})^{\rm H}]</math>

For complex random vectors, another matrix called the '''pseudo-cross-covariance matrix''' is defined as follows:

:<math>\operatorname{J}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{cov}(\mathbf{Z},\overline{\mathbf{W}}) \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ \operatorname{E}[(\mathbf{Z}-\mathbf{\mu_Z})(\mathbf{W}-\mathbf{\mu_W})^{\rm T}]</math>

==Uncorrelatedness==
{{main|Uncorrelatedness (probability theory)}}
Two random vectors <math>\mathbf{X}</math> and <math>\mathbf{Y}</math> are called '''uncorrelated''' if their cross-covariance matrix <math>\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{X}\mathbf{Y}}</math> matrix is a zero matrix.<ref name=Gubner>{{cite book |first=John A. |last=Gubner |year=2006 |title=Probability and Random Processes for Electrical and Computer Engineers |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-86470-1}}</ref>{{rp|p=337}}

Complex random vectors <math>\mathbf{Z}</math> and <math>\mathbf{W}</math> are called uncorrelated if their covariance matrix and pseudo-covariance matrix is zero, i.e. if <math>\operatorname{K}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = \operatorname{J}_{\mathbf{Z}\mathbf{W}} = 0</math>.
